title: How To Handle Misbehavior The First Two Weeks Of School st-two-weeks/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explains why new students test their teacher's boundaries around the second week of school, arguing this is driven by students' uncertainty about the teacher rather than defiance for its own sake. He offers a sequence of specific responses for when testing occurs: pausing before reacting, concealing disappointment, being willing to 'lose the battle' of a confrontation, and calmly following through with the stated consequence. Additional guidance covers moving on immediately after enforcing a consequence, not taking misbehavior personally, and handling incidents personally rather than sending students to the office. Throughout, the piece frames restrained, steady enforcement as the path to being seen as a trustworthy leader rather than a pushover. It ends by tying disciplined early responses to the larger goal of building a 'dream class' for both teacher and students.
points: Take a deliberate pause of about twenty seconds before responding to misbehavior instead of reacting immediately.
Never show hurt or disappointment over misbehavior; keeping composure signals control and prevents students from finding an emotional lever.
Be willing to 'lose the battle' in the moment rather than lecture or argue, in order to win long-term influence over students.
State the consequence plainly and tie it to the specific rule broken, then move on immediately so misbehavior barely registers.
Handle testing incidents yourself rather than sending students to the office, since ownership is what establishes a teacher as a leader worth following.
quotes: Maybe some of your students have never had firm boundaries. Maybe they’ve never known an adult they could look up to and count on . Maybe they’ve never had a teacher they liked or even trusted.
Your first reaction to misbehavior should be no reaction. Don’t rush over and put a stop to it. Don’t call out and try to interrupt it. Just wait, observe, and let it play out.
If a student is directing his (or her) misbehavior toward you, disrespects you, or talks back to you, be willing to take it. Resist the urge to lecture , scold, or put the student in his place.
Turn your attention away from the student and continue on with what you were doing. Leave to him the responsibility to get back to work or walk to time-out.
Misbehavior in the beginning of the school year is about your students and their experiences with teachers and adults in the past. It’s not about you.
They take misbehavior personally. They begin reasoning with students. They threaten, scold, and raise their voice. They dole out false praise and unworthy rewards.
